claims.text: High-entropy alloys can be designed to improve melting temperature, fusion enthalpy, fusion entropy, melting volume change, and liquid-phase thermodynamic properties by optimizing composition and processing.
AlCoFeNi is an example of a high-entropy-alloy initial state.
NbMoTaW is an example of a high-entropy-alloy initial state relevant to the proposal.
Varying alloy composition can alter phase stability and microstructure in AlCoFeNi-based alloys.
Changing annealing conditions can alter phase decomposition and its length scale in AlCoFeNi-based alloys.
Substitution of Co by Cr in AlCoFeNi promotes decomposition into ordered B2 and disordered BCC phases.
High-temperature conditions can induce structural and chemical evolution, phase separation, and melting in high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles.
High pressure is an applicable condition for obtaining the proposed thermodynamic-property improvements.
Selective laser melting or spark plasma sintering can produce the proposed thermodynamic-property improvements.
The effects of composition and processing are mediated by formation of solid solutions, precipitates, or other microstructural features.
Configurational entropy influences phase formation and the relevant thermodynamic behavior of high-entropy alloys.
Enthalpy of mixing influences solid-solution formation and phase stability in high-entropy alloys.
Atomic-size differences influence solid-solution stabilization in multicomponent high-entropy alloys.
Composition and processing optimization will increase melting temperature or reduce entropy of fusion.
Existing high-entropy alloys provide baselines with known thermodynamic properties.
Current processing techniques or accessible composition ranges limit applicability of the proposed approach.
Complex interactions among composition, processing, and microstructure make thermodynamic properties uncertain to predict.
A lack of correlation between measured thermodynamic properties and predictions based on configurational entropy and mixing enthalpy would falsify the hypothesis.
